58013.summary:
The 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy Statement, adopted 20 February 2026. Two things stand out. First, the pivot: internal borrowing runs from £129.9m at 31 March 2026 to £30.9m in 2027, then £0 from 31 March 2028 onwards (Table 8, para 6.22). The 2025/26 strategy had assumed external borrowing would resume in 2025/26; higher-than-forecast cash balances have deferred it a year (para 7.4). But from 2027/28 the DSG deficit — £193.2m at 31.3.26, £289.2m at 31.3.27, £413.9m at 31.3.28 (para 6.16, Table 7) — consumes the cash previously funding internal borrowing (58009 preamble). External borrowing for the capital programme has to take over.

Second, the strategy against that pivot is deliberately short-then-long. Paragraph 6.10 is explicit: new external in 2026/27 up to five years on maturity or EIP structures, then switch to long-term (up to 50 years) 'when borrowing costs are forecast to fall from their current elevated levels'. It is a dated bet on long rates falling, taken on MUFG's Appendix B forecast (Appendix B not in the extracted text). Meanwhile, no borrowing in advance of need in 2026/27 (para 6.25). £142.9m of new external is required in 2026/27 either way.

The statutory override on the DSG deficit ends 1 April 2028; the Autumn Budget Statement (2025) confirmed that from that point the deficit transfers to central government budgets. The Provisional Settlement acknowledged the pressure and 'confirmed support will be available for historic deficits', details awaited (para 6.20).

Balance-sheet identity CFR − external borrowing − PFI/leases = internal borrowing closes exactly across 2025/26, 2026/27 and 2027/28 (see checks). Loan-book reconciliation ties to the pound at 31 March 2026 — 31 PWLB loans in our file, £437.2m against their Table 5 figure of £437.2m, weighted rate 4.03% consistent with the interest budget.

summary.text:
Every figure in the paper reconciles, including the loan book to the pound at 31 March 2026 (31 PWLB loans / £437.2m / 4.03% weighted, against the paper's £437.2m in Table 5). The strategy is where the interest is.

West Sussex has been running an internal-borrowing strategy since 2010 (para 6.21). It ends in 2027/28. Internal borrowing falls from £129.9m at 31.3.26 to £30.9m in 2027 to £0 from 31.3.28 (Table 8) because the DSG deficit consumes the cash that used to fund it — £193.2m at 31.3.26, £289.2m at 31.3.27, £413.9m at 31.3.28, then held (para 6.16). The statutory override ends 1 April 2028 and the Autumn Budget Statement (2025) confirmed DSG will move to central government budgets from that point.

The strategy against that pivot is a deliberate short-then-long. Paragraph 6.10 says new external in 2026/27 will be up to five years (maturity or EIP), and long-term borrowing (up to 50 years) will be switched into 'when borrowing costs are forecast to fall from their current elevated levels'. £142.9m of new external is needed in 2026/27, of which £84.6m is Economic Developments; another £166.8m follows in 2027/28 — £149.0m Core plus £17.8m Economic Developments (Table 8). It is a dated, falsifiable position priced on MUFG's Appendix B forecast (Appendix B not in the extracted text).

No LOBOs, no exceptional financial support, no capitalisation direction, no s114. Standard MRP-and-CIPFA shape underneath.

loan_book_reconciliation.text: Our PWLB file at as-at=2026-03-31 returns 31 loans totalling £437,240,300 at a weighted 4.0305% (30 MATURITY, 1 EIP). Paper Table 5 (para 6.15) prints existing PWLB debt at 31 March 2026 of £437.2m. Match to the pound (rounded). Weighted rate also ties: Table 10 (para 6.24) puts the 2026/27 existing-PWLB interest budget at £17.6m; on the £437.2m book that implies ~4.03% average — matches 4.0305%.

balance_sheet_identity.text: CFR − external borrowing (excl PFI/leases) − PFI/finance leases = internal borrowing. Closes across three years to £0.0m rounding. 2025/26: 677.7 − 444.2 − 103.6 = 129.9 ✓ (Table 8: 129.9). 2026/27: 708.4 − 582.4 − 95.1 = 30.9 ✓ (Table 8: 30.9). 2027/28: 788.9 − 703.1 − 85.8 = 0.0 ✓ (Table 8: 0.0). Sources: Table 4 (para 6.13) for CFR, Tables 5 and 7 (para 6.15) for external borrowing excl PFI, Table 4 for PFI/finance leases, Table 8 (para 6.22) for internal borrowing.

borrowing_requirement_buildup.text: Table 3 (para 6.11): internal £129.9m + capital programme £58.5m + refinance PWLB maturity £4.7m − MRP £16.4m − financing applied £2.9m = £173.8m total requirement. New external £142.9m + internal £30.9m at 31.3.27 = £173.8m funding. Sums exact.

gross_external_debt_composition.text: Table 5 (para 6.15) external borrowing 31.3.26 = £444.2m (PWLB £437.2m + CHC short-term £7.0m). Table 4 (para 6.13) PFI/finance leases 31.3.26 = £103.6m. Sum £547.8m matches Table 8 (para 6.22) Gross External Debt 31.3.26 opening (£578.3m less repayments and PFI amortisation to £547.8m closing — confirmed by the movement table).

cfr_projection_composition.text: Table 4 (para 6.13) splits: Core Borrowing CFR £490.6m + Economic Developments CFR £83.5m + PFI/leases £103.6m = £677.7m at 31.3.26. Sums exact across all six years. Table 6 (para 6.15) 'Loans CFR' = CFR − PFI/leases: 677.7 − 103.6 = 574.1 ✓ ; 708.4 − 95.1 = 613.3 ✓ ; 788.9 − 85.8 = 703.1 ✓ .

dsg_cashflow_arithmetic.text: Para 6.17: DSG deficit 'does equate to a potential loss of £241.3m in average cash balances in 2026/27 which is a loss of investment income of £8.3m'. £8.3m/£241.3m = 3.44% implied yield — sits comfortably with the paper's 3.42% average Bank Rate forecast for 2026/27 (para 8.1).

authorised_limit_composition.text: Table 12 (para 6.30) 2026/27: Capital Borrowing £781.6m + Cashflow Borrowing £0m + PFI/leases £95.1m = £876.7m ✓ . 2025/26 as approved Feb 2025 was £940.5m (higher because it carried £40m unexpected-cashflow headroom now moved into the LB's £40m liquidity buffer, footnote iii).

existing_pwlb_repayment_walk.text: Para 6.9: PWLB £461.3m at 31.12.24 → £456.9m at 31.12.25 → £24.1m repayable in full year 2025/26. £461.3m − £24.1m = £437.2m matches Table 5's 31.3.26 figure exactly. Implied Q4 2025/26 repayment of £456.9m − £437.2m = £19.7m.

reference_rates.text: PWLB notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026, CERTAINTY rates (published standard less 0.20): 1y 4.95%, 2y 5.06%, 5y 5.34%, 10y 5.83%, 20y 6.38%, 25y 6.46%, 50y 6.27%. Bank Rate 3.75%. OIS 1y 4.11%, 2y 4.21%. July 2026 sector PWLB activity: £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%. Same reference set as the batch of drafts written 14 August 2026.

internal.break_cost_indicative: On the DMO's 14 Aug 2026 premature repayment curve (notice 314/26 PM), all 31 of our live loans price to £379.625m against a £437.240m balance — a net £57.616m indicative DISCOUNT, 13.2% of principal. 15 loans sit below par (mainly the five super-long PWLBs at 2.12%-2.32% totalling £125m and £62m in indicative discount) and 16 above (mainly the mid-2020s vintage at 4.80%-4.95%). Not raised in the email as a suggestion: the paper's Table 3 shows every pound of internal borrowing is already spoken for by the DSG cashflow shift, and paragraph 6.35 says rescheduling 'may be considered ... but only if there is surplus cash available'. There is not. Recorded here for completeness; if the officer asks, we can walk it.
internal.loan_book_dec_2025_gap: Paper para 6.9 says PWLB at 31 December 2025 was £456.9m. Our file at as-at=2025-12-31 returns 19 loans / £272.6m — a £184m gap driven by the known bc-loans Start-date issue (some loans have Start dates later than their true drawdown, so they don't appear outstanding on historical as-at queries). This is why the reconciliation used in the email is at 31 March 2026 (£437.2m to the pound), which reads correctly on both sides. Do not quote the £456.9m position against our file.
internal.appendix_b_missing: Para 6.10, 6.25 and 8.1 reference MUFG Corporate Markets' interest rate forecasts in Appendix B. Appendix B was not extracted with 58013.raw.txt and is not held. The paper's short-then-long strategy is priced against those forecasts — without Appendix B we can quote the Bank Rate assumption (3.75% held to 31.3.26, two cuts to 3.25% by 31.3.27, average 3.42% through 2026/27; para 8.1) but not the paper's long-end trajectory. Do not attribute a specific PWLB-rate view to MUFG that we cannot see in the paper.
internal.capital_strategy_missing: The MRP policy sits in the Capital Strategy report (paras 6.13, 2.3-2.4), not in the TMSS. Only the 2026/27 MRP estimate (£16.4m, Table 3) appears in the paper we've read. Do not quote any MRP methodology.
internal.s151_identity: Signatory is Mike Suarez, Executive Director of Finance and Support Services (end of the paper, before Contact Officers). The paper does not describe him as the Section 151 Officer in terms, though by role for a county council of this shape he almost certainly is. Do not assert the S151 title without external confirmation. Contact Officers named at the end are Vicky Chuter, Financial Reporting Manager (033 022 23414) and Jon Clear, Treasury Management Officer (033 022 23378) — neither published with an email address.
internal.commercial_investments: The paper carries two investment properties (para 7.47) held since 2018/19 within the former Coast to Capital LEP boundary, and an equity holding in the UK Municipal Bond Agency plc (para 7.47). Also a JV with Kinsted LLP (formerly Lovell Partnerships) via the wholly-owned Edes Estates Ltd, with a £0.4m revenue loan rising by £1m in 2026/27 (para 7.50). Not raised — none of this is a treasury-first hook and the paper handles all of it under its Capital Strategy separation.
internal.no_officer_email: No officer email address is published anywhere in the three extracted files. The email is written to be sent but has no recipient — it will need an address before it ships. This is the same block that Bedford, Buckinghamshire and other TMSS-only councils sit under in the pipeline.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to County Council on 20 February, six months in. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, because it settles whether the rest is worth reading. We hold 31 PWLB loans for West Sussex totalling £437.24m at a weighted 4.03%, against the £437.2m in your Table 5 at 31 March 2026. That is a match to the pound, and the weighted rate ties as well — Table 10 puts the 2026/27 existing-PWLB interest budget at £17.6m, which is 4.03% of the same book. Everything below sits on top of that reconciliation.

We wrote because of the pivot the strategy describes.

You have run an internal-borrowing strategy since December 2010 (para 6.21). On the numbers in Table 8 it ends in 2027/28. Internal borrowing falls from £129.9m at 31 March 2026 to £30.9m in 2027 and to zero from 31 March 2028 onwards. The reason is not the capital programme — it is the DSG deficit consuming the cash that used to fund the internal borrowing. Paragraph 6.16 gives the trajectory in terms: £193.2m at March 2026, £289.2m in 2027, £413.9m by March 2028, then held. The statutory override ends 1 April 2028, and the Autumn Budget Statement (2025) confirmed the deficit moves into central government budgets from that date. Paragraph 6.17 puts the 2026/27 investment income foregone at £8.3m on £241.3m of average cash balances lost to the deficit — the cash cost of the transition, in one number.

Paragraph 6.10 sets out the strategy against that pivot, and it is a deliberate short-then-long. New external in 2026/27 up to five years on maturity or EIP structures, then switch to long-term (up to 50 years) 'when borrowing costs are forecast to fall from their current elevated levels'. £142.9m of new external is needed in 2026/27 either way — of which £84.6m is Economic Developments — and Table 8 shows another £166.8m following in 2027/28 (£149.0m Core, £17.8m Economic Developments). The strategy has priced against MUFG's Appendix B forecast, which we don't hold, and so we won't quote it back. What we would offer instead is the shape of the two objects the bet sits on.

On the short end: today (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August), one-year PWLB certainty closed at 4.95%, two-year 5.06%, five-year 5.34%. The market's own implied path is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity alongside the SONIA forward curve — SONIA has the one-year at 4.11% and the two-year at 4.21%, which is what is priced rather than what anyone forecasts, and it is the object that tells you whether waiting is cheap or expensive at the short end. Your paragraph 8.1 assumes Bank Rate averages 3.42% through 2026/27 on two cuts to 3.25% by March; Bank Rate is still 3.75% at 14 August, so the cuts are running to the assumption rather than ahead of it. Same tool covers July's sector borrowing (£368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, average 5.02%) — the depth of the market on the days you'd actually be in it.

On the long end, we deliberately don't publish forecasts. What we do publish is your book against the DMO's premature repayment curve daily, and where each of the paragraph 6.10 alternatives sits on it. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — with the note that paragraph 6.35 already prices this correctly for you (rescheduling only where surplus cash is available, and Table 8 says there isn't any from 2027/28 onwards).

One page we'd genuinely point you to for this strategy specifically is pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark. It rebuilds your Table 7 shape — the £582.4m 2026/27 benchmark against £432.5m of maturing PWLB, and the crossing point — against live rates rather than the ones in the paper, and lets you drag the internal-borrowing profile through it.
